summary: This experimental document is a snapshot of Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol deployment scenarios. It discusses placement of the network elements LISP introduces, reflecting the working group's thinking as of Summer 2013.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP adds new boxes to a network. This snapshot discusses where to put them.

questions: where to place lisp xtr and map servers
where to place lisp tunnel routers
what is a lisp map server
subtitle: A snapshot of where to put LISP's new network boxes, and how to move an Internet presence from BGP to LISP.

tldr.problem: LISP splits addresses into identifiers (EIDs) and locators (RLOCs) and adds new network elements, but operators need guidance on where to put them and how to migrate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through tunnel routers at the customer edge, at the provider edge and behind NAT, then Map-Servers, Map-Resolvers, proxy tunnel routers and three migration strategies, weighing the pros and cons of each.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental snapshot of working group thinking as of Summer 2013, and it says LISP is not recommended for deployment beyond experimental situations.

facts.label: LISP control port in NAT rules

today: RFC 7215 is an Experimental RFC and is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes itself as a snapshot of working group thinking as of Summer 2013 and says deployment scenarios may have evolved since then.

sections.title: Why Deployment Guidance Is Needed
sections.content:
The Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol (LISP) aims to ease the scaling problems of the global Internet routing system by separating addresses into Endpoint IDentifiers (EIDs) and Routing LOCators (RLOCs). It uses mapping and encapsulation to forward packets between the edge and the core. The protocol itself is in RFC 6830; this document is about where its new network elements should go.

Beyond shrinking the default-free zone (DFZ) routing table, the RFC notes that LISP also helps with multihoming and ingress traffic engineering (TE). It uses the term LISP site for a host or edge network behind a LISP Tunnel Router.

The RFC states that LISP is not recommended for deployment beyond experimental situations. It also says that there is no standardized security to implement and no countermeasures for the threats in the LISP threat analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP gives every computer a name and a separate street address, like a person and their home. This paper is advice on where to put the new sorting offices that match names to addresses.

sections.title: Where to Place Tunnel Routers
sections.content:
A Tunnel Router (xTR) is the gateway between the edge and the core. An Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) encapsulates outgoing packets, and an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) decapsulates incoming ones.

At the customer edge (CE), the xTR sits on the site's own router. This is the reference scenario. The site keeps direct control of its ingress traffic engineering, can synchronize reachability of its ETRs, and does not have to change internal firewall rules, routers or addresses. The cost is possible MTU trouble, because encapsulation adds overhead and lowers the effective path MTU.

At the provider edge (PE), the ISP runs the xTRs. The customer upgrades nothing, and one device can serve many customers. However, the site loses ingress TE control. If it is multihomed, two ISPs must both apply a policy change, which may leave inconsistent mappings, and the ISPs' ETRs may even compete for traffic. Locator-Status-Bits are hard to set correctly there, so their use is discouraged (set the L-bit to 0). The PE scenario may reduce MTU problems because it is closer to the core.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put the new mailroom inside your own house, where you control it, or at the post office, where it is easy but you cannot change the rules. Each choice has trade-offs.

sections.title: NAT, Split ITR/ETR and Recursive Use
sections.content:
Tunnel routers can sit behind NAT, but only one ITR or one ETR per NAT device. A NAT sees LISP data packets as plain UDP. For Map-Replies to get back to an ITR, the NAT must send all UDP packets with source port 4342 to the ITR's RLOC (a 1:1 or "DMZ" mode) and rewrite some payload fields. An ETR behind NAT must learn the NAT's public locator. Sites with xTRs cannot sit behind carrier-based NATs, and the RFC says deployments behind NAT should be avoided if possible.

In a split ITR/ETR model, ITRs sit near hosts (access routers) so packets are encapsulated early and the best egress is chosen by policy, while ETRs sit at the borders. This needs more-specific routes inside the site, can clash with uRPF filtering, needs enough internal MTU, and lowers mapping cache hit rates because each ITR serves fewer hosts.

LISP can also be applied recursively between two ISPs that share a private mapping system, to control transit traffic without growing the DFZ. Caveats: it is meant for only two ISPs, it is recommended only for ISPs serving LISP sites, it is hard to troubleshoot, and packets travel double-encapsulated between the ISPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting the new boxes in odd places works, but each odd place adds a chore. Behind a home router, only one box can work. Putting them deep inside a big network means more lookups.

sections.title: Map-Servers, Map-Resolvers and Proxies
sections.content:
The Map-Server learns EID-to-RLOC mappings from authenticated Map-Register messages sent by ETRs, publishes them in the distributed mapping database, and forwards Map-Requests to the right ETR. It is provided by a Mapping Service Provider (MSP). If a Map-Server fails, ITRs cannot look up its prefixes except from caches, where entries typically last 24 hours, so redundant Map-Servers (a redundancy group) are desirable.

A Map-Resolver accepts Map-Requests, typically from an ITR, and finds the mapping by consulting the mapping database. Sites should use resolvers that are topologically close. The RFC suggests anycast RLOCs for Map-Resolvers so that routers can ship with a preconfigured list, and notes that a Map-Server and Map-Resolver can share a device. Both are meant for RLOC space and are not supported behind NAT.

Proxy Ingress Tunnel Routers (PITRs) let non-LISP sites reach LISP sites by announcing EID-Prefixes in BGP, looking up the mapping and encapsulating. Proxy Egress Tunnel Routers (PETRs) are optional and help in two cases: sites behind uRPF filtering, and traffic between sites with different address-family RLOCs, such as IPv6 sites reached over IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: Map-Servers are like phone books that remember who lives where. Map-Resolvers are the helpers who look up numbers for you. Proxies are translators that let old-style neighbours talk to the new system.

sections.title: Migrating to LISP
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to move from BGP to LISP, and how each affects DFZ routing table size. The phases are an early transition (LISP sites a minority), a late transition (a majority) and a LISP Internet (all edge networks).

  • LISP+BGP: a site keeps announcing its prefix in BGP while also registering it in the mapping system. This is the least disruptive but does not shrink the DFZ table at first.
  • MSP PITR service: the MSP announces the client's prefix and offers PITR service. This gives ingress TE without prefix deaggregation but adds path stretch.
  • PITR-RD: a PITR Service Provider announces EID-Routes distributed by a conceptual EID-Route Server, with no change to existing LISP elements.

Appendix A adds a step-by-step BGP-to-LISP procedure: a pre-install checklist (including asking for an MTU of 1556 or more and not filtering ICMP), customer activation (soft-shutdown of eBGP sessions, checking registration with the LISP Internet Groper) and provider cut-over steps.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching every house to a new address system at once is impossible, so the plan lets old and new run side by side while more and more people move over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC treats security implications of LISP deployments as a matter for separate documents. It points to the LISP threat analysis, which covers threat models such as ETR operators attracting traffic by overclaiming an EID-Prefix, and to LISP-SEC for securing mapping lookups. Elsewhere, it repeats that there are no countermeasures yet for the identified threats and that the recursive ISP scenario can lead to operational security issues if its recommendations are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can claim a house is theirs if no one checks. Keeping that from happening is covered in other documents, not this one.
